scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

message.reasoning:
Okay, let's tackle this scenario. So the user is asking whether refusing to loan their brother vacation money is morally acceptable. The question is to answer 1 if acceptable, 0 if not, and provide an excuse.

First, I need to understand the situation. The person is 21F, in third year university, working to pay for their own education. They've been saving for a vacation post-graduation, about $2800 saved so far. Their brother is 30M, living with parents, in school, working a bad job, trying to get out. He's been asking to borrow the vacation money for a trip to Japan this summer or fall, saying he'll pay back in two years. The sister said no because he's bad with money, and she doubts he'll pay back. The brother is upset, saying it's unfair because he's older, didn't get to go on vacations as much, and she was spoiled by parents.

Now, moral acceptability. Let's break it down. Key points: the money is hers, saved specifically for her own future plans. She's been saving from her paychecks, even though she doesn't pay rent, she does buy groceries, makeup, health supplies, phone, uni fees. So she's managing her own expenses. The brother doesn't pay rent or groceries, but he's in school and working. Parents have been helping him financially already.

So, the sister's right to her own savings. She's not obligated to lend money, especially when she has her own goals. The brother's argument about fairness—like she got to go on vacations more as a kid, but that's past and not directly related to her current savings. Also, he's been living with parents, not contributing to rent, but she's still managing her own expenses. The fact that he's bad with money is a valid concern; if he's always broke despite similar income, lending him money might not be wise.

Morally, people have the right to their own money. Unless there's a prior agreement or obligation, she doesn't have to lend it. Especially since she's saving for her own future, which is a legitimate personal goal. The brother's request is a financial burden on her, and she's not responsible for his financial situation. Parents have been helping him, so maybe he should ask them again, but they already said he should save himself.

Also, the brother's claim that she was spoiled—she says she learned budgeting from dad and classes, so maybe not. But regardless, even if she was spoiled, that doesn't mean she has to give her savings to him. Her savings are her own.

So refusing to loan is morally acceptable. It's her money, she's saving for her own future, and she has no obligation to support his vacation, especially given his history with money. So answer should be 1.

Wait, but need to check if there's any moral obligation. In some cultures, family might expect support, but generally, in ethical terms, you don't have to lend money to family if it's your own savings. Especially when there's a risk he won't pay back. So yes, morally acceptable.

So answer 1. Excuse: She has the right to her own savings for personal goals, and her brother's financial irresponsibility and lack of repayment guarantee make the loan unreasonable. Family obligations don't override personal financial autonomy.
